title: Validation-driven Deployment of LLM Inference Platforms for Agentic Workloads
org: Shai Gretz and co-authors, with the llm-d team
authors: Shai Gretz, Alon Halfon, Yoav Katz and 10 others
gist: A pipeline for validating an agentic serving stack from first test to production, using recorded sessions replayed with their content, live agent runs and synthetic load. Replay holds each session's token load within 1.18x of the recording; re-running the agents drifts up to 4.98x. Rolling out four large mixture-of-experts models on llm-d, traffic recorded on the target model reached about 60% of the throughput public traces had suggested, and exposed a routing bug they hid.
changes: The first report of a stack sized on public agent traces and then checked on traffic from its own model. The public traces overstated capacity by about 1.7x and hid a routing bug. That leans T4 toward the traffic, and makes capture the first part of the rig to build.
caveats: The recorded traffic is benchmark tasks run by real agents on the target model, not customers' sessions; production was checked only against token-length histograms. The authors put the gap down mainly to answer lengths and session shapes that follow the model. One team, H100 and H200, and the 60% is a rough figure across four models. The coverage analysis sees only vLLM's Python code.

numbers.metric: Per-session input tokens at the 95th percentile, against the recording
numbers.baseline: live re-runs of the same agents, up to 4.98x

numbers.metric: Per-GPU throughput on traffic recorded from the target model
numbers.baseline: the same stack on public agent traces from SemiAnalysis and NVIDIA
numbers.setup: GLM-5.3, Nemotron 3 Ultra, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Kimi K3 on llm-d, H100 and H200

bears_on.note: Public traces misjudged capacity by about 1.7x and hid a routing bug; live, replayed and synthetic tests each reached code the others missed.
Traffic generated by the target model halved the operating point found on someone else's traces.
Your own traffic matters for sizing and for catching bugs. The paper does not show per-customer tuning beating a class-level stack.
